title: Why You Should Never Ever Be Friends With Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin's perennial classroom-management argument that 'friendship energy' from teacher to student causes a cascading set of management problems and undermines the very respect-and-warmth relationship teachers are reaching for when they try to be friends. The piece distinguishes between the mature, kind, professional regard that students need from a teacher and the peer-style friendliness that erodes classroom authority. When teachers chase friendship, students stop reading the structure of the room as stable; behaviors that should be quietly redirected become repeated, and the teacher pays for the informality with louder corrections later. Linsin's positive frame: students do not need a friend (they have those), they need a calm, predictable, fair, dignified adult who likes them, holds the line, and teaches them well. The relational warmth a teacher should bring is not friendship; it's the warmth of a trusted adult who uses authority on the student's behalf. points: 'Friendship energy' from teacher to student creates a cascading management problem: students stop reading the room's structure as stable, and small misbehaviors compound that should have been quietly redirected.
Students don't need another friend — they have those. They need a calm, predictable, fair, dignified adult who likes them, holds the line, and teaches them well.

The warmth a good teacher brings is the warmth of a trusted adult using authority on the student's behalf, not the casual closeness of a peer; one strengthens classroom culture, the other undermines it.

Chasing friendship usually buys the teacher louder corrections later because the small redirections that maintain calm classrooms only work when the teacher's role is clearly distinct from student-peer roles.
Mature professional regard, not informality, is the foundation of the relationship students will look back on as formative.
